Senses.Explanation: The step beyond the top of a hundred-foot pole, where the image leaves no footing for another step. The fixed phrase and case title are drawn from Changsha Jingcen's verse: the person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole, although having gained entry, is not yet real; the verse then requires a step forward and says that the worlds in the ten directions are the whole body (百尺竿頭坐底人，雖然得入，未為真；百尺竿頭須進步，十方世界現全身). Wumen Huikai's Case 46 titles the case Stepping Forward from the Pole-top and attributes the question “atop a hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?” to Shishuang Qingzhu (石霜和尚云，百尺竿頭如何進步). Fojian Huiqin's later verse explicitly names Old Changsha at the time of the pole-top step (百尺竿頭進步時……老長沙). The phrase then circulates as a public question: Yexian Guixing answers “the southern continent, the northern continent” (南贍部洲，北欝單越), Linye Qi answers “then retreat” (退後即得), and Shanduo Zhenzai answers “a beheaded boatman goes down to Yangzhou” (斷頭船子下揚州). Langye Huijue places the pole-top step beside a saying with no intent in the phrase and no phrase in the intent, then asks how to breathe out. Zen bends the impossible ordinary action into a named case, a quoted verse-line, and a repeatedly answered public question; the records give different answers without changing the action denoted.
